messages.content: How does the Bahá'í concept of the soul differ from the Hindu and Buddhist concepts of reincarnation? I want a sharp answer — not 'all religions teach about the soul' but the actual ontological differences.

The Bahá'í teachings state that individual human souls do not return to this physical world in new bodies, preserving instead a single earthly life and an enduring, distinct individuality after death. The sources here do not provide sufficient comparative material to detail the specific Hindu and Buddhist ontological frameworks beyond noting that the Hindu concepts of reincarnation and metempsychosis are considered erroneous.

The core distinction is that while the soul progresses and develops, its essence and reality do not cycle back into earthly bodies.

That passage says the Bahá'ís accept a "return of the attributes and qualities" but not of "the essence or the reality of things" — but what does that distinction actually mean ontologically, and isn't it close to the Buddhist view that no essence transmigrates, only a causal stream of qualities?

The sources here do not settle whether the Bahá'í distinction between returning qualities and an unreturning essence mirrors the Buddhist teaching of a causal stream without an enduring soul, as the texts I can search do not discuss Buddhist ontology in detail.

Here is how the texts describe this return:

- ["The Bahá'í view of 'reincarnation' is essentially different from the Hindu conception. The Bahá'ís believe in the return of the attributes and qualities, but maintain that the essence or the reality of things cannot be made to return."](https://oceanoflights.org/lights-of-guidance-baha-i-ocean-en/#:~:text=The%20Bah%C3%A1'%C3%AD%20view%20of,%7Bid%3D%22para6868%22%20ilmid%3D%22bl4jb%22%20type%3D%22par%22%20language%3D%22en%22%7D) — *Lights of Guidance* quoting Universal House of Justice
- [“'Return' does not refer to 'specific, individual souls and identities'.”](https://bahai-library.com/2845/?paraId=h21) — *Reincarnation, Rebirth and the Progress of the Soul*
- [“The essence of a thing is known through its qualities; otherwise, it is unknown and hidden.”](https://bahai-library.com/4481/?paraId=h116) — *The God of Baha'u'llah*
- [“It is the return of the qualities.”](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/doris-mckay_memories-of-bahais#p1116) — *Memories of Bahá’ís* as recalled by Doris McKay
- [“...by this is only intended the return of the qualities, character, perfection, truth and Lights... and not (the return) of certain persons and spirits.”](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/abdul-baha_tablets-on-reincarnation-and-imperfection-in-creation#p12) — *Tablets on Reincarnation and Imperfection in Creation* by ‘Abdu'l-Bahá

These passages share the perspective that spiritual influence, character, and divine lights recur across different ages and individuals, while distinct personal identities and individual essences remain permanently separate.

You say the distinction is that individual identity and "the essence or the reality of things" "remain distinct and do not return" — but the Shoghi Effendi passage never mentions the soul or individual identity there; it says "Every being keeps its own individuality" about things generally, in a passage about reincarnation. Isn't equating "essence" with the individual soul your interpretation rather than what the text says, and is the lamp-and-flower analogy (cited via a pilgrim's recollection) really authoritative enough to carry that weight?

Let us look strictly at what the sources actually state, separating them by their kind.

**What scripture says**
The central texts speak of the reality of things and their individuality rather than defining the soul's essence through analogies.

**What authorized interpretation says**
In explaining the "return" mentioned in scriptures, the interpretation clarifies that "The Bahá'í view of 'reincarnation' is essentially different from the Hindu conception. The Bahá'ís believe in the return of the attributes and qualities, but maintain that the essence or the reality of things cannot be made to return." — *Lights of Guidance* quoting Universal House of Justice.

**What history and scholarship add**
Historical and scholarly studies note how these concepts intersect with wider mystical frameworks, such as Sufi discussions of annihilation (*faná'*) and subsistence (*baqá'*), where [“After the seeker has reached the ultimate point, either his individuality is annihilated in God ( fanā   ) or he descends and returns to the world without being separated from God (baqā   ).”](https://siftersearch.com/library/islam/history-and-biography/oliver-scharbrodt_islam-and-the-bahai-faith#p72) — *Islam and the Baha'i Faith* by Oliver Scharbrodt.

Does keeping "individuality" and "essence" distinct in the text alter how you read the parallel with the Buddhist causal stream?

You cite Shoghi Effendi's line that the soul keeps "developing and unfolding and returning towards its Creator" while rejecting return to new bodies. How does that compare with the Hindu view of the ātman returning to Brahman, which also ends in union with the source? Does the Bahá'í text actually give a reason why individuality survives that return, when Advaita says it dissolves?

You are right to point to that parallel, for both traditions speak of an upward movement toward a divine source. In the Hindu texts, the goal is often described through the realization of identity with the ultimate reality, where Ramanuja’s commentary on the Vedanta-Sutras discusses the whole world as springing from Brahman and returning to it as the Self of the world ([The Vedanta-Sutras with Ramanuja Commentary (SBE Vol. 48)](https://oceanlibrary.com/hymns-of-atharva-veda)).

The Bahá'í writings describe a continuous journey where the soul, after its separation from the body, ["will continue to progress until it attaineth the presence of God, in a state and condition which neither the revolution of ages and centuries, nor the changes and chances of this world, can alter."](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_474&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_fx.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_fx.1978) — *Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh*.

Does the Bahá'í text explain why individuality survives this approach to the Creator? The texts point to the origin of the soul itself: rather than being a temporary spark that merges back and loses distinction, "the rational soul is endowed from the beginning with individuality; it does not acquire it through the intermediary of the body." ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_834&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_q4.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_q4.602)) — *Some Answered Questions*. Because that individuality is inherent and primary rather than bodily, its approach to God is described as an unending progression in nearness rather than an absorption that erases the distinct self.

Where Advaita sees the drop returning to the ocean to become the ocean entirely, the Bahá'í texts see a mirror growing ever clearer while remaining a mirror. How do you see those two images comparing when you look at the texts side by side?

wordings.text: You said evil is "much as cold is the absence of heat or darkness the absence of light." How does that compare with Augustine's formulation in the Enchiridion (ch. 11) or Plotinus's treatment of evil in Ennead I.8, and do the Bahá'í texts themselves ever acknowledge that lineage?

messages.content: Do the Bahá'í writings handle evil as the mere privation of good (Augustinian), as an active force, or as a necessary shadow that makes good visible?

The Bahá’í writings speak of evil primarily as a privation or lack—akin to darkness being the absence of light—while acknowledging its experiential reality and connection to the lower human nature.

Here is how the texts and authorized interpretations address this:

*   ["It is thus evident that all evil is mere non-existence. Good has a positive existence; evil is merely its absence."](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_924&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_sl.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_sl.95) — *Some Answered Questions* by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá
*   ["Evil is imperfection. Sin is the state of man in the world of the baser nature..."](https://oceanlibrary.com/paris-talks_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_1042&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-paris-talks_en_vp.0~abdu-l-baha-paris-talks_en_vp.644) — *Paris Talks* by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá
*   ["Then it is evident that in creation and nature evil does not exist at all; but when the natural qualities of man are used in an unlawful way, they are blameworthy."](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-world-faith-abdul-baha-section_2/?paraId=para_301&selectionString=baha_i_world_faith_en-blbo.0~baha_i_world_faith_en-blbo.991) — *Bahá’í World Faith* by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá
*   ["We know absence of light is darkness, but no one would assert darkness was not a fact. It exists even though it is only the absence of something else. So evil exists too..."](https://oceanlibrary.com/unfolding-destiny_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_3925&selectionString=unfolding_destiny_bahai_ocean_en-bl3kl.0~unfolding_destiny_bahai_ocean_en-bl3kl.316) — *Unfolding Destiny* by Shoghi Effendi

These passages share the perspective that while evil lacks an independent, positive essence of its own—manifesting instead as a deficiency, darkness, or misdirected human capacity—it remains a palpable reality in human experience that must be actively recognized and supplanted by good.

Regarding the first one you quoted: is that actually from Some Answered Questions, and which chapter and whose translation? I'd also like to know whether 'mere non-existence' renders a particular Persian or Arabic term, because that wording sounds distinctly Augustinian.

The passage is indeed from *Some Answered Questions* by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, found in Chapter 73, "Pre-Existence and Origination" (or Chapter 72 in some editions). The translation is by Laura Clifford Barney, who recorded and translated the tablet.

Regarding your challenge about the Augustinian phrasing: the translation "mere non-existence" renders the Persian phrase *‘adam-i maḥ* (عدم محض), meaning "pure non-existence" or "absolute non-existence."

The passages only provide the question heading for Chapter 73 in English and one Persian fragment on origination: *Qadím va ḥādiith chand qism ast?* (قديم و حادث چند قسم است ؟) from *Reincarnation (original, Persian)* by ‘Abdu'l-Bahá ([Reincarnation (original, Persian)](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/core-tablets/abdul-baha_reincarnation_fa#p2)).
